Boycott

/BOY-kot/ — rhymes with apricot · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To boycott something is to deliberately refuse to buy, use, or take part in it, usually as a form of protest.

Customers boycotted the store until it improved working conditions.

Worked Example

Environmental groups called for a boycott of products from the oil corporation, urging consumers to shop elsewhere until the company committed to cleaner practices.

Boycott is precise here because it names not just refusing to buy, but doing so deliberately and collectively as organized pressure—a protest tactic. 'Refuse' is too plain and doesn't capture the group action and protest motive that make boycott powerful.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

abstain: To abstain is to choose not to take part — a quiet, individual decision, like sitting out a vote, made with no plan to pressure anyone. To boycott is the opposite of quiet: an organized, public refusal designed to force a company or institution to change.

snub: To snub someone is to reject or ignore them pointedly in a personal, social way — refusing a handshake, skipping an invitation. A boycott is not personal but collective and economic: a group deliberately refuses to buy or take part until the target changes its ways.

protest: To protest is to object publicly — marches, chants, signs, and letters all say that something is wrong. A boycott is one particular way of protesting that goes past words: people refuse to buy or use something until the target gives in and changes.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

patronize: to regularly buy from or support a business

endorse: to publicly support or approve of something

Where it sits · how organized and public the protest is — avoid → shun → refuse → boycott

avoid vs. boycott: Avoid is much weaker than boycott: avoiding a store just means quietly steering clear of it, while a boycott is a deliberate, organized act of protest.

shun vs. boycott: Shun is stronger than avoid but still weaker than boycott — shunning is pointedly keeping away, while a boycott turns that refusal into public, collective action.

refuse vs. boycott: Refuse is a firm personal 'no,' but boycott goes further: a boycott is a refusal made as an organized protest, often by a whole group acting together.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — Boycott

Root — Boycott: from Captain Charles Boycott, an Irish land agent ostracized by the Irish Land League in 1880 for refusing to lower rents (English (eponym))

Put it together

Put it together: Boycott doesn't break into word parts — it is an eponym, a word made from a person's name. In 1880, the community around Captain Charles Boycott refused to work with him, trade with him, or even speak to him, and his name became the word for exactly that kind of organized refusal.

Use the root in a new word: boycotter

Use the root in a new word: boycotter: The boycotters stood outside the shop with signs, urging every customer to join their boycott until the owner treated workers fairly.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral to formal

Boycott names the specific tactic of organized refusal as protest—reach for it when discussing collective action against a company or cause. For personal avoidance, use 'avoid' or 'refuse.'
